title: #CourageON: As COP31 continues, young advocates hope the world will listen
summary: Although not in Antalya, Franciene Enriquez and Mak Bogabong are still keeping an eye on the negotiations, watching out for decisions that could impact their communities

blocks.text: As world leaders and negotiators gather in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate talks, climate advocate Franciene Enriquez hopes someone there is listening.

The negotiations, which began on November 9, are taking place amid wars and growing concerns over fossil fuel dependence. While the energy crisis has renewed arguments for shifting to cheaper clean energy, fossil fuel interests continue to influence the talks.
Civil society organizations and climate advocates are also using the conference to campaign, rally, and press governments to act, bringing the stories of affected communities into the discussions.

While Franciene won’t be attending COP31, she’s waiting for these calls to be actually heard. “We’ve been here for a long, long time…. Hindi kami nabibigyan ng liwanag (We are not being given a chance to be seen).”
Franciene is the founder of Kabataan para sa Kalikasan ng Atimonan and a climate advocate and community facilitator with the Philippine Movement for Climate Justice.

Growing up in Atimonan, Quezon province, she saw how energy development affected communities around her: large trucks interrupting children’s play, families being displaced, dark patches appearing in the sea, and mountains being cut open.

These experiences pushed her to organize against destructive projects, including the proposed Atimonan One Energy coal-fired power plant. In a feature in November 2025, we told Franciene’s story of championing renewable energy, alongside the stories of fellow climate advocates Joshua Villalobos and Mak Bogabong. In the same month, we also wrote about how communities opposed the proposed Atimonan coal plant.
Now in her early twenties, Franciene feels frustrated that her community’s concerns and stories remain in the dark, even after more than 30 years of annual climate negotiations.

“Nakakainis lang, nakakagalit, nakakadismaya kung bakit kapag may mga ganitong usapin lang siya na-bi-bring up (It’s frustrating, infuriating, and disappointing that these issues are only brought up during discussions like COP).”

For Franciene, what happens on the ground is not given enough attention. Speaking out about it, however, comes with risks, including being hunted down or red-tagged. She sees this as part of a wider conflict: companies profit from coal projects, while communities bear their consequences.

On Mak’s side of the country, it’s quite a different story. He is based in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, where awareness of climate change and international climate talks like COP remains limited. Much of his work begins with reaching out to communities and getting them involved in conversations about the climate crisis.

blocks.caption: REPRESENTATION. Mak Bogabong is the sole representative from BARMM at the Mindanao Stakeholders’ Consultation for the Philippines’ Just Transition Framework held in Davao City on September 25-26, 2025. Photo from DENR

blocks.text: Mak is part of JetX Bangsamoro under Reboot Philippines, a youth-led organization advocating for a just transition to renewable energy. He’s also part of ILAYA, or Intergenerational Leaders Advancing Youth for Climate Action, which brings together not just young people but also older generations to work on environmental and climate issues.
“We’re trying to embrace everyone in this advocacy,” Mak said. He shared, with a wide grin, how ILAYA has grown from three members to 15, with a new batch expected to bring its numbers past 20.

ILAYA has organized activities bringing together grade school and high school students to discuss climate change and its effects. Mak was struck by how they responded, even with limited prior knowledge.
“When faced with reality that is inevitable, a reality that is there, a reality that has something to do with your life and death, these young people, the way they think, it’s just amazing,” he said.

blocks.caption: CLIMATE IMMERSION. Mak Bogabong engages in discussions on renewable energy and just transition with Bulacan residents during Reboot Philippines’ immersion activity. Photo from Reboot Philippines

blocks.text: He believes civil society organizations like JetX Bangsamoro can help harness young people’s energy and give them opportunities to act. He won’t be attending COP31 himself, but he hopes the conference will create more opportunities for these groups to participate in climate discussions and decisions.

He also recognizes that political power shapes COP, yet he wants to remain hopeful. “I don’t really have a choice but to be really hopeful,” he said. “A little bit cynical, still…. I want to put myself in the position to remain hopeful.”

Franciene shared that sentiment. The young people in her community often look to her for answers, and she feels she has to keep going for their sake. Although not in Antalya, both she and Mak are still keeping an eye on the negotiations, watching out for decisions that could impact their communities.

blocks.caption: GLIMMERS OF HOPE. Franciene Enriquez speaks with members of KAPAKANAN during a group discussion. Photo by Franciene Enriquez

blocks.text: “I have to be optimistic,” Franciene said. “Kasi, if hindi, anong mangyayari (Because if I’m not, what’s going to be the result of that)?”

“Kailangan mo dito ng malakas na loob (You need courage to do this),” she added. “Wala man akong maayos na sagot na makuha from them (Even if I don’t get a proper answer from the climate negotiations), I will push through to have that answer that I’m seeking.” – Rappler.com

#CourageON is a bi-monthly newsletter providing updates from our communities. In time for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), the month of November features stories of courage and resilience from our partner communities and advocates.
